about: Hot Springs bonus words. Every form must be a legal dictionary word (tools/check-lexicon.mjs). Tiers pay +10 / +15 / +25. Each entry's fact comes from the audited bank (bank id) or quotes a research file (ref + quote); tools/check-facts.mjs verifies both.

fact.text: The Fordyce basement shows spring number 46 beneath a glazed-tile arched ceiling.
USGS dating puts most Hot Springs thermal water at about 4,400 years old.
"Valley of Vapors" comes from the steam rising off the springs.
fact.quote: nickname for the steam rising off the springs
fact.src: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Hot Springs; npshistory.com

fact.text: The town's old nickname, the Valley of Vapors, comes from the steam off the springs.
fact.quote: nickname for the steam rising off the springs
fact.src: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Hot Springs; npshistory.com

fact.text: Tufa is the white-to-tan rock that the springs' dissolved minerals leave around their openings.
Travertine, or tufa, builds up where minerals precipitate around the spring openings.
Novaculite, the Ouachita whetstone rock, takes its name from the Latin for "razor stone."
Novaculite whetstone mining began in the Hot Springs region as early as 1818.
Quartz crystal became Arkansas's state mineral in 1967.
Arkansas named quartz crystal its state mineral in 1967.
Hotel Hale's 9 suites have soaking tubs fed with hot springs mineral water.
Rain soaking into Bigfork Chert and Arkansas Novaculite outcrops recharges the thermal springs.
Silica is the thermal water's second most plentiful constituent, after bicarbonate.
Bicarbonate is the most concentrated constituent of the thermal water, ahead of silica and calcium.
Hot Springs Creek flows through a tunnel beneath Bathhouse Row.
The government enclosed Hot Springs Creek in an underground arch in 1882-83.
The DeSoto Fountain sits directly beneath the Fordyce's stained-glass skylight.
A jug fountain was installed in front of the park's Administration Building in 1966.
Congress established the Government Free Bathhouse on Dec. 16, 1878.
In 1920 a standard prescribed course was 21 baths.
Its bathing industry made Hot Springs known as the "Great American Spa."
An 1877 railroad booklet sold Hot Springs as America's Baden-Baden.
Hotel Hale's 9 suites have soaking tubs filled with hot springs mineral water.
The Quapaw Bathhouse was built with a 40-tub capacity.
In 1920, towels and robes cost extra on top of the bath attendant's fee.
fact.quote: towels, robes and mercury rubs extra

fact.text: In 1920 a bath attendant's fee was capped at 20 cents a bath.
James Truman (Arlington, 1922) and Estella Hughey (Majestic, 1926) were among the first Black masseurs and masseuses.
fact.quote: were among the first Black masseurs and masseuses
fact.src: NPS: African Americans and the Hot Springs Baths

fact.text: A pre-1915 Maurice booklet lists terrazzo floors and white-marble bath partitions.
The Maurice advertised white-marble bath partitions in a booklet from before 1915.
The Maurice once boasted a glass-and-steel-domed solarium with Caen stone walls.
fact.quote: a glass-and-steel-domed solarium with Caen stone walls

fact.text: A massive stained-glass skylight crowns the Fordyce men's bath hall.
The Quapaw is crowned by a large tiled dome topped with a copper cupola.
A small copper cupola tops the Quapaw's chevron-mosaic dome.
The Quapaw's dome is covered in a chevron mosaic of tile.
The 1922 Ozark Bathhouse has twin towers and a vague Art Deco look.
Work on the Grand Promenade behind Bathhouse Row began in the 1930s.
Robert Stevens laid out the Magnolia Promenade in the 1890s with double rows of magnolias.
fact.quote: laid out by Robert Stevens in the 1890s with double rows of magnolias
fact.src: NPS: Bathhouse Row National Historic Landmark nomination; Cultural Landscape Inventory

fact.text: Two bronze federal eagles guard Bathhouse Row's 1890s main entrance.
The Hot Springs Reservation became Hot Springs National Park on March 4, 1921.
The 1832 Hot Springs Reservation predates Yellowstone by 40 years.
The steel Rix Tower of 1906 carried visitors to the top by elevator.
The lattice-steel Hot Springs Mountain Tower stands 216 feet tall.
Central Avenue was originally called Valley Street.
Carpenter Dam, completed in 1931, formed Lake Hamilton.
Phase One of the Northwoods trail system is 14 miles long.
Rainbow trout are stocked below Carpenter Dam from November through April.
H. L. Campbell founded the alligator farm in 1902 as a tourist draw.
Hot Springs' alligator farm dates from 1902.
Thomas Cockburn opened the Ostrich Farm in 1900; it closed in 1953.
The IQ Zoo's founders helped train pigeons for Project Pigeon in WWII.
The first Arkansas Derby, in 1936, carried a $5,000 purse.
Politics forced the Oaklawn racetrack to close in 1907; it reopened in 1916.
Oaklawn's Jockey Club formed in 1904.
Oaklawn's Racing Festival of the South, created in 1974, runs a stakes race each day.
In 2017 HANA ranked Oaklawn 5th among North American thoroughbred tracks.
fact.quote: HANA ranks Oaklawn 5th among North American thoroughbred tracks

fact.text: The George Barr school (1935–47) in Hot Springs was baseball's first umpire school.
Babe Ruth's 1918 homer at Whittington Park landed in an alligator farm.
Babe Ruth hit his famous 1918 Hot Springs homer in the sixth inning.
In the 1930s Al Capone rented an entire floor of the Arlington Hotel.
The former Southern Club casino at 250 Central Avenue now houses a wax museum.
In 1963 reporters photographed the Vapors nightclub's slot machines and craps tables.
Capone reportedly played poker at an elevated table in the Southern Club.
In 1967 Gov. Winthrop Rockefeller ordered the State Police to crack down on gambling.
A 1937 single-player electromechanical pinball machine was titled "Hot Springs."
The elegant Eastman Hotel had about 500 rooms.
Diamond Jo Reynolds's railroad cut the 21-mile trip from Malvern to about an hour.
The World's Shortest St. Patrick's Day Parade had its first grand marshal in 2004.
Labor Day weekend brings jazz and blues shows downtown.
By 1928 the McClards were cooking goat with their barbecue sauce.
A used roller coaster bought for $10,000 in 1991 cost close to $900,000 to relocate.
The thermal springs produce over 700,000 gallons of water a day.
The springs emerge at the base of Hot Springs Mountain at about 143°F.
fact.quote: emerge at the base of Hot Springs Mountain at about 143

fact.text: The Goat Rock Trail on North Mountain climbs from 886 to 1,067 feet.
The CCC built Lake Catherine State Park in the 1930s; three stone-and-wood cabins are on the National Register.
In 2004 Smarty Jones won Oaklawn's $5 million centennial bonus.
The original Hot Springs Railroad from Malvern ran on 3-foot narrow gauge.
A tufa cavity found while digging the Quapaw was promoted as a cave, and gave the bathhouse its name.
Owney Madden came to own a controlling interest in the Southern Club on Central Avenue.
In 1946 a record 649,270 baths were taken on Bathhouse Row.
The Hot Water Hills Music and Arts Festival is held at Hill Wheatley Plaza.
In 1927 William Jacobs encased the Southern Club's front in dark Pittsburgh glass.
The Superior's facade is concrete painted to look like ornamental tile, with green medallions.
The Maurice's 1931 therapeutic pool was inspired by FDR's treatments at Warm Springs, Ga.
The maple-leaf oak grows wild at only four sites in the world, all in the Ouachita Mountains.
KTHS radio aired its inaugural program from the ballroom on Dec. 20, 1924.
Babe Ruth's long home run of March 17, 1918, landed in the alligator farm.
Tiny Town's miniature trees are made from cat-food cans and wire.
Scalloped shells frame the sculpin fish on the Quapaw's parapets, originally gold and now white.
The Fordyce was the first bathhouse to close, in 1962, and became a visitor center and museum.
Garvan Woodland Gardens covers 210 acres on Lake Hamilton.
Anthony Chapel, of wood and glass, opened in Garvan Woodland Gardens in September 2006.
A small copper cupola tops the Quapaw's tiled dome.
A life-size de Soto statue stands in the Fordyce men's bath hall; most historians discredit the legend that he visited.
At the IQ Zoo, opened in 1955, trained chickens walked tightropes; rabbits, ducks and raccoons performed too.
The Great Fire of Sept. 5, 1913, began when an iron set a curtain alight.
In the 1913 fire, Little Rock's hoses arrived by train around 8 p.m. but didn't fit the local hydrants.
